about: Pages of the experiment scratchbook. Title, question, status, tags and links come from data/projects.json (by projectId); this file holds the page content. Each experiment fills one two-page spread. layout picks the page composition (pasted, printout, flow, plot, equation; see style.css 'Scratchbook layouts'). sketch names an SVG in assets/sketches/ drawn beside the figure. openQuestion is an optional question printed on the page. Run `node tools/build-catalogue.mjs` after editing.

experiments.headline: A little chaos

figure.alt: The Lorenz attractor plotted in three dimensions: two looping lobes traced by a single trajectory.
figure.caption: 5,000 steps from (0.01, 0.01, 0.01), plotted with Matplotlib.

experiments.equation: ẋ = σ(y − x)   ẏ = x(ρ − z) − y   ż = xy − βz
experiments.explanation: Three coupled equations with σ = 10, ρ = 28 and β = 8/3, stepped with forward Euler at dt = 0.01. The notebook also covers phase space and the Van der Pol oscillator.
experiments.observation: The trajectory never repeats and never settles, yet it stays on the same two-lobed shape. Bounded but unpredictable was the idea I wanted to see.
experiments.note: chaotic is not the same as random
experiments.openQuestion: How quickly do two starting points 10⁻⁵ apart stop agreeing?

gallery.alt: The Lorenz trajectory projected onto the x–z plane: two loops joined in a butterfly shape.
gallery.caption: x against z

gallery.alt: x over time for two runs that start 0.00001 apart; the two curves match until about t = 14, then separate.
gallery.caption: Two starts 10⁻⁵ apart part ways near t = 14

experiments.headline: Everything pulls on everything

figure.caption: Velocity Verlet, as written in the repository: the force is recomputed between the position and velocity half-steps.

experiments.explanation: Particles fall toward a point with an inverse-square pull (softened below a distance of 5 so nothing divides by zero), bounce off each other with elastic collisions, and stay inside a sphere. Rendered with OpenGL; released for macOS, Linux and Windows.
experiments.observation: Velocity Verlet averages the old and new accelerations, so it needs the force evaluated twice per step. That ordering is the whole difference from the semi-implicit Euler loop in the fluid simulation.
experiments.note: compare with the fluid sim's integrator
experiments.sketchCaption: The three steps of one update, in the order the code runs them.

experiments.headline: Reading the quiet genome

figure.alt: Funnel chart from the Myelovar web interface showing how many variants survive each pipeline stage.
figure.caption: Stage-by-stage variant counts from the pipeline's own funnel view.

experiments.explanation: Seven stages, s0 to s6. Load the variants, drop common ones, keep those inside 18 ENCODE regulatory tracks from MM.1S myeloma cells, score transcription-factor motif disruption in a ±30 bp window, link each element to a target gene, weigh myeloma relevance with DepMap CRISPR data, then rank.
experiments.observation: Most of the work was making each filter explainable. Every surviving variant carries a plain-English evidence chain, so a reader can see which stage kept it and why.
experiments.note: research use only, not a diagnostic

gallery.alt: The Myelovar review page: a variant funnel from 3,935,734 to 48,113 variants beside the Motif Ledger title, labelled illustrative sample data.
gallery.caption: The review page, on sample data

experiments.headline: An assistant I can read

figure.caption: The permission policy. Anything that leaves the machine can never be set to run without approval.

experiments.explanation: An Electron and TypeScript assistant that can run a local model through Ollama or Claude through the API. Every tool is tagged with a scope; reads run freely, while file deletions, shell commands and anything external wait for a click. A pause switch denies every call until it is turned off.
experiments.observation: Writing the policy as a small class with its own tests made the safety rule something I could check, rather than something I hoped the model would follow.
experiments.sketchCaption: DEFAULT_RULES from the policy file, drawn as a flow.

experiments.headline: Watching a model learn

figure.alt: Three scatter plots of house price against square footage, bedrooms and bathrooms, with one predicted house highlighted in orange.
figure.caption: Normal-equation fit on house_prices.csv; the orange point is the prediction for 2,100 sq ft, 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms.

experiments.explanation: Linear regression by gradient descent and by the normal equation, plus logistic regression, written with NumPy and pandas instead of a machine learning library.
experiments.observation: The normal equation gives the answer in one line of linear algebra, which made it obvious what gradient descent is iterating toward.

gallery.alt: Scatter plot of scaled house price against square footage: actual prices in one shade, the model’s guesses in another along a rising band.
